content: The wheelchair I use allows me to move freely on the court without restricting my left leg, which enhances my stability and minimizes discomfort. This design boosts my confidence, enabling me to improve my performance and fully enjoy the sport. A single wheelchair model or size cannot meet the diverse requirements of all users. A limited selection may result in inappropriate devices for most individuals. Member States should aim to provide a range of manual and powered wheelchairs, cushions, postural supports, and other accessories to address the varied needs of users in different contexts. Documenting the most suitable equipment, funding options, and the consequences of not providing the recommended device can help prioritize products and plan services effectively. For example, collaboration between UN agencies, such as WHO and UNICEF, has increased the availability of affordable, high-quality assistive products. WHO has developed specifications for 26 priority assistive products, including wheelchairs, and published a procurement manual with UNICEF to guide countries in their procurement processes. These resources also signal manufacturers and suppliers about minimum requirements for assistive products. New products have been added to the UNICEF and WHO supply catalogues to enhance global access to quality assistive devices at affordable prices. Wheelchairs come in various designs to meet different user needs. They can be manual (propelled by the user or an attendant) or powered (using a motorized source). Some are designed for specific activities, such as sports or navigating rough terrain, while others address unique needs like stair climbing. Regardless of the design, all wheelchairs aim to provide mobility, seating, postural support, and functional assistance. Selecting the right combination of features is crucial to meet each user’s needs optimally. Liberia, for instance, developed its first National Priority Assistive Products List (APL) in 2021 as part of a strategy to improve access to assistive technology. This initiative, led by the Ministries of Health and Gender, Children, and Social Protection, along with the National Commission on Disabilities and disability organizations, adapted WHO’s priority list to reflect local needs and resources. The final APL included two types of manual wheelchairs among 33 assistive products. This list serves as a foundation for further actions, such as developing technical standards, quality checklists, service delivery guidelines, and advocating for funding and training. Some regions and countries adapt these standards to their specific contexts. For example, Europe and Australia/New Zealand have established overall product standards for manual wheelchairs based on ISO testing. Preparation involves assembling the wheelchair and accessories, inspecting them for safety, and making initial adjustments. This process may involve multiple adjustments and appointments, especially for users with complex needs. Proper fitting prevents product abandonment and secondary injuries. Training is essential for wheelchair users and their assistants to maximize the device’s benefits. Training includes skills for using the wheelchair, operating its components, guiding others, and performing maintenance and repairs. For example, users may learn to transfer in and out of the wheelchair, navigate different environments, and maintain the device. Training should be tailored to the individual’s needs, goals, and environment. Peer trainers, particularly those with lived experience, can play a valuable role in providing relatable and effective training. In Kenya, a peer training initiative supports individuals with spinal cord injuries during their rehabilitation. Peer trainers, who are wheelchair users themselves, provide guidance on mobility skills, health, and rights. This program empowers both trainers and participants, improving quality of life and rehabilitation outcomes.
